Heavily slanted WSJ article on new mortgage laws

Posting this on Voat because I work for a mortgage lender and have been heavily involved in implementing changes to these laws. But I'm pretty sure my employer wouldn't be happy about me publicly talking about some of this. So, I'm trying to provide general information rather than how we're specifically trying to support this.

First, the article implies that the law is just disclosure form simplification. Believe me- if that was the case, this would have taken a couple of weeks to do. Less, maybe. But this is barely a footnote in the difficulty of implementing these new regulations.

The CFPB has redefined a "mortgage application". Unfortunately, now a "mortgage application" doesn't include enough information to write a loan. Even though, the lender now has three days to disclose a loan, despite not necessarily having enough information to write one. Typical government bullshit there.

Secondly, tolerances in fee variances has gone to zero. Which, at first, seems a good thing. Except that lenders don't control all the fees. Like insurance rates. We have to accurately disclose them despite not having control over the final number. But the lender now carries all legal responsibility for disclosure. If the insurance company changes rates, it's our fault. Not theirs.

There are a few other things, but believe me- the industry hasn't been dragging its feet. It's been trying to figure out how to implement rules that may not be quite possible to implement. And will be costly to support. Any variance will restart the lending process- not only delaying the loan, but also costing more to "fix".

The sky isn't falling. I'd wait a bit before buying a house, but these new laws aren't going to kill off the industry. But crap like this doesn't even come close to trying to tell the real story.
